extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing screenwriters (beginner to seasoned) who want to outline feature-length screenplays
extracted.subtask_short: planning screenplay with Save The Cat
extracted.subtask_description: Create a Save The Cat beat sheet — a 15-beat, page-mapped outline for a feature-length screenplay — to plan story structure, character arcs, and pacing before writing the script.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is a beat sheet
rubrics_metrics.description: A beat sheet is a summarized or condensed version of your screenplay, made up of 'story beats' — key story events and scenes that impact the story or the characters; it functions as a blueprint of your entire story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the beat sheet to outline your screenplay in detail; think of beats as the essential story events that change character states or push the plot forward. The article frames the Save The Cat beat sheet as an expanded, page-mapped evolution of the classic three-act structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening Image (page 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The very first thing the audience sees; helps set the theme or mood of the screenplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an opening image that establishes tone and theme (e.g., an eerie shot of the haunted house in a horror movie). Though it may seem insignificant, it sets the audience's initial expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme Stated (page 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A moment, usually around page 5, where the theme of the film is communicated (often by a character) in a single scene beat; it's the ultimate takeaway you intend the audience and characters to have by the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the Theme Stated moment clear and memorable (Blake Snyder: 'The Theme Stated moment of a movie is vital; it's what your movie is about'). Example: Jack's 'Make each day count' in Titanic. The Theme Stated often seeds the protagonist's later revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Set-up (pages 1-10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce the important parts of the screenplay within the first 10 pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure you introduce: the protagonist's status quo (current life and surroundings), the protagonist's main goal, and any characters relevant to main story beats (or at least hint at them). This establishes baseline stakes and context for the inciting events.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Catalyst (page 12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Also called the inciting incident; the single story beat that changes the character's status quo and sets off the main story — the start of the point of no return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place a clear, compelling event around page 12 that decisively disrupts the status quo and forces the protagonist toward a new trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Debate (pages 12-25)
rubrics_metrics.description: A section where the protagonist struggles with doubt and asks 'What should I do next?'; they are reluctant to accept the call to action or go on the journey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use internal and/or external obstacles to justify the protagonist's hesitance; this builds character motivation and makes the eventual choice meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break Into Two (page 25)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moment the protagonist overcomes doubt (or is forced) and makes the choice to begin the main journey — the bridge between Act One and Act Two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make this turning point decisive and visible (example: Neo's red pill/blue pill choice in The Matrix). It should clearly push the story into the 'new world' or main conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: B storylines (page 30)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce subplots around page 30 that add dimension and usually involve a character who helps the protagonist learn an important life lesson or the theme of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly a love interest, mentor, or platonic friend; the B story often provides emotional grounding and a means for the protagonist to internalize theme-related lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fun & Games (pages 30-55)
rubrics_metrics.description: Also called 'The Promise of the Premise' — the part of the story that delivers what was promised to the audience (the hook), where the protagonist navigates the new world and the story delivers its core pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this section to explore the premise's possibilities; it's the 'meat' of the story where genre expectations are satisfied and the protagonist's new life is showcased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midpoint (page 55)
rubrics_metrics.description: The halfway beat where stakes are raised and the protagonist experiences either a false victory or a false defeat, establishing a new goal or conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This should be a dramatic turning point (example: the chest-bursting scene in Alien) that changes the trajectory and escalates stakes; treat it as a mini-climax that reframes Act Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Bad Guys Close In (pages 55-75)
rubrics_metrics.description: The phase where, following the Midpoint, things go worse (if there was a false victory) or appear to improve (if there was a false defeat); internal and external pressures build against the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase obstacles and antagonistic forces here, allowing both external antagonists and the protagonist's internal flaws to converge and tighten the stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: All Is Lost (page 75)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist's lowest point in a single story beat: they receive a huge blow, lose everything gained, or realize gains are meaningless; often includes a mentor's death or symbolic 'death of the old hero.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage a clear, devastating reversal that makes the protagonist's situation seem irretrievable; this heightens emotional investment and sets up the ensuing introspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark Night of the Soul (pages 75-85)
rubrics_metrics.description: A period of deep hopelessness where the protagonist wallows and undergoes introspection, unable to immediately climb out of despair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this beat to let the protagonist reflect, mourn, or reassess — it prepares the audience for the protagonist's reveal/decision in the next beat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break Into Three (page 85)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist's 'aha!' moment — usually stemming from the theme stated earlier — which gives them renewed strength and leads into Act Three.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the revelation feel earned and connected to the Theme Stated; it should logically motivate the protagonist to try again with new understanding (example: Elle's revelation in Legally Blonde).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Finale (pages 85-100)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act Three sequence where the protagonist faces the main conflict again and demonstrates that they've internalized the story's theme to resolve the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose a final confrontation that proves character growth (overcoming misunderstanding, defeating adversary by applying the theme) and resolves primary plotlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Final Image (page 100)
rubrics_metrics.description: The last thing the audience sees before the credits; it should reflect how much the protagonist has changed over the journey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a closing image that contrasts with the Opening Image to show transformation (e.g., protagonist in an improved life, empowered, or with a new appreciation for life).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical production: use a template and proper screenplay formatting (JotterPad/Fountain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beat sheets and screenplay outlines can be written in software using templates; JotterPad provides a Save The Cat template and supports Fountain markup to export properly formatted screenplays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided template (replace bolded text; grey header/synopsis won't export) to build your beat sheet and then write the screenplay using Fountain syntax for scene headings, character names, dialogue, transitions, and correct margins/format. This is a practical tip for moving from outline to properly formatted script.
